questions.q: One mole of a monatomic ideal gas undergoes the process $\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{B}$ in the given $p$ - $V$ diagram. Specific heat capacity in the process is
questions.solution:
According to the question,
Now, the temperature at point $A$ and $B$ By, $p V=n R T$ (from ideal gas equation) Temperature at point $A$, T_A=\frac{3 p_0 V_0}{R} Temperature at point $B$, T_B=\frac{30 p_0 V_0}{R} So, the temperature difference, $\Delta T=T_B-T_A$ \begin{array}{ll} \therefore & \Delta T=\frac{30 p_0 V_0}{R}-\frac{3 p_0 V_0}{R} \\ \text { or, } & \Delta T=\frac{27 p_0 V_0}{R} \end{array} or, Now, due to the adiabatic process, change in internal energy, \therefore \quad \Delta U=n C_v \Delta T
Work done by the gas undergoes the process \begin{aligned} & A \rightarrow \mathrm{B} . \\ & \therefore W=\text { Area under } p \text { - } V \text { graph } \\ & \text { or } \quad W=18 p_0 V_0 \end{aligned}
Now, by first law of thermodynamics, Q=\Delta U+W By putting the values from Eqs. (i) and (ii) to above Eq. we get \begin{array}{lcl} \therefore & Q=\frac{3}{2} R \Delta T+\frac{2}{3} R \Delta T \\ \text { or } & C \Delta T=\frac{13}{6} R \Delta T \\ & (\because Q=n C \Delta T, \text { where } n=1 \text { mole }) \\ \text { or } & C=\frac{13}{6} R \end{array} So, the specific heat capacity in the process $A \rightarrow B$ is $C=\frac{13}{6} R$.

questions.q: One mole of an ideal diatomic gas undergoes a process as shown in the figure. The molar specific heat of the gas in the process is
questions.solution:
In the curve, $V \propto \frac{1}{T}$
$\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow V=m \frac{1}{T} \text { where, } m=\text { slope of curve. } \\
& \Rightarrow V T=\text { constant } \\
& \therefore \quad T d V+V d T=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad d V=-\frac{V}{T} d T \\
& \text { As, } Q=\Delta U+W \\
& C d T=C_V d T+p d V \\
& C d T=C_V d T-\frac{p}{T} V d T \\
& \Rightarrow \quad C=C_V-\frac{p V}{T} \\
& =C_V-R \quad\left(\because \frac{p V}{T}=R\right) \\
&
\end{aligned}$
For diatomic gas, $C_V=\frac{5}{2} R$
$\therefore \quad C=C_V-R=\frac{5}{2} R-R=\frac{3 R}{2}$

Both statement-I and statement-II are correct

Assertion (A): Gases do not liquify above their critical temperature even on applying high pressure.
Reason (R) : Above critical temperature molecular speed become high and inter molecular attractions can not hold molecules together.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of \(A\)
Both A and R are true but R is not correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.solution:
- Assertion (A) is true because gases do not liquefy above their critical temperature, no matter how much pressure is applied. This is because above the critical temperature, the kinetic energy (or speed) of the gas molecules is too high for intermolecular forces to bring them close enough to form a liquid.
- Reason (R) is also true and correctly explains the assertion, as above the critical temperature, the molecular speed is high, and intermolecular attractions are too weak to hold the molecules together, preventing liquefaction.

Pressure is proportional to the square of velocity (whether RMS or mean or most probable, just the constant of proportionality changes).
Hence (i) and (ii) are false.
Rate of diffusion is proportional to the mean speed, (this is true)
The average kinetic energy is proportional to temperature in the kelvin scale.
Hence, statement (iii) and (iv) are true.

B. Each degree of freedom is associated with 12RT average energy per mole.

C. A monoatomic gas molecule has 1 rotational degree of freedom where as diatomic molecule has 2 rotational degrees of freedom

D. CH4 has a total to 6 degrees of freedom.

Choose the correct answer from the option given below:
questions.solution:
According to the equipartition of energy, each degree of freedom carries 12RT energy per mole and total energy per mole of a gas having n degrees of freedom is 12nRT. Therefore, statement A is wrong and statement B is correct.

A monoatomic molecule only has translational degrees of freedom and does not have rotational degree of freedom. For a polyatomic model there are three rotational degrees of freedom and three translational degrees of freedom. Therefore, statement C is incorrect and statement D is correct.

Consider the following statements related to the Kinetic Theory of Gases:

- Statement 2: False. Gases behave ideally at low pressures and high temperatures.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:

  List I   List II
(A) 3 Translational degrees of freedom (I) Monoatomic gases
(B) 3 Translational, 2 rotational degrees of freedoms (II) Polyatomic gases
(C) 3 Translational, 2 rotational and 1 vibrational degrees of freedom (III) Rigid diatomic gases
(D) 3 Translational, 3 rotational and more than one vibrational degrees of freedom (IV) Nonrigid diatomic gases

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The formula for degree of freedom is given by 

f=3N-k

where N is the number of particles, k is the individual relationship in the system.

For a monoatomic gas particle, N=1, k=0. So, f=3

Hence, monoatomic gas has 3 translational degree of freedom.

For a rigid diatomic gas molecule, there are 5 degrees of freedom, 3 translational and 2 rotational. A diatomic gas can have two extra degrees of freedom due to rotation along two independent axes.

A non rigid diatomic molecule has one extra degree of freedom than a rigid one. This is the vibrational degree of freedom. Hence, it has 6 degrees of freedom.

So, a non rigid diatomic gas has 3 translational, 2 rotational and 1 vibrational degrees of freedom.

A polyatomic gas has more than two atoms per molecule. Hence, the total number of degrees of freedom is 3 translational,  3 rotational and more than one vibrational degree of freedom.

questions.q:
Match the quantities in Column I with their corresponding expressions in Column II.
\(\begin{array}{|c|l|c|l|}
\hline
& \text{Column I} & & \text{Column II} \\
\hline
(a) & \text{Root mean square speed} 
  & (p) & \tfrac{1}{2} m v_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2} = \tfrac{3}{2} k_{B} T \\
\hline
(b) & \text{Mean free path} 
  & (q) & \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi d^{2} n}} \\
\hline
(c) & \text{Ideal gas equation} 
  & (r) & P V = n R T \\
\hline
(d) & \text{Degrees of freedom} & (s) & 5 \\
  & \text{of a diatomic gas}  &  & \\
\hline
(e) & \text{Pressure of an ideal gas} 
  & (t) & P = \tfrac{1}{3} \rho v_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2} \\
\hline
\end{array}\)
questions.solution:
1. (a) Root mean square speed corresponds to the relation where the kinetic energy is given by \(\frac{1}{2} m v_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\frac{3}{2} k_B T\), which shows the connection between temperature and molecular speed.
2. (b) Mean free path is the average distance a molecule travels before colliding, and it is given by \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi d^2 n}}\), where \(d\) is the diameter of the molecules, and \(n\) is the number density.
3. (c) Ideal gas equation is represented by the familiar equation \(P V=n R T\), which relates pressure, volume, and temperature of an ideal gas.
4. (d) Degrees of freedom of a diatomic gas is typically 5, accounting for 3 translational and 2 rotational degrees of freedom at normal temperatures.
5. (e) Pressure of an ideal gas is related to the root mean square speed by \(P=\frac{1}{3} \rho v_{\mathrm{rms}}^2\), where \(\rho\) is the density of the gas.

questions.q:
Match the concepts in Column I with the related physical quantities or expressions in Column II.
\(\begin{array}{|c|l|c|l|}
\hline
& \text{Column I} & & \text{Column II} \\
\hline
(a) & \text{Average kinetic energy} & (p) & \tfrac{3}{2} k_B T \\
  & \text{of gas molecules}  &  & \\
\hline
(b) & \text{Internal energy of} & (q) & U = \tfrac{3}{2} n R T \\
  & \text{an ideal gas}  &  & \\
\hline
(c) & \text{Kinetic theory of gases} & (r) & \text{Random motion of molecules} \\
\hline
(d) & \text{Maxwell-Boltzmann} & (s) & \text{Distribution of} \\
  & \text{distribution}  &  & \text{molecular speeds} \\
\hline
(e) & \text{Degrees of freedom} & (t) & 3 \\
  & \text{for a monatomic gas} &  & \\
\hline
\end{array}\)
questions.solution:
1. (a) Average kinetic energy of gas molecules is given by \(\frac{3}{2} k_B T\), where \(k_B\) is the Boltzmann constant and \(T\) is the temperature, showing that kinetic energy is directly proportional to temperature.
2. (b) Internal energy of an ideal gas for a monatomic ideal gas is \(U=\frac{3}{2} n R T\), where \(n\) is the number of moles and \(R\) is the gas constant.
3. (c) Kinetic theory of gases deals with the random motion of molecules and how it relates to macroscopic properties like pressure and temperature.
4. (d) Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution explains the distribution of molecular speeds in a gas and predicts how many molecules have a particular speed at a given temperature.
5. (e) Degrees of freedom for a monatomic gas are 3, all of which are translational, as monatomic gases have no rotational or vibrational degrees of freedom at normal conditions.
